highlights: PHI rebuilt on daily Apple Watch data — four pillars: Recovery, Sleep, Activity, Fitness
Re-based so 100 = Mike's 2023–2025 normal; the latest reading is 108 (8% above baseline)
The legacy sleep/activity/weight index is preserved as PHI-Classic — no published number was rewritten
The series now reaches back to January 2023 (versus late 2025 before)

narrative.executiveSummary:
The Personal Health Index has been rebuilt. The original PHI was a simple monthly estimate — sleep, activity, and weight, often hand-tallied. With a complete daily record now flowing from Apple Watch, PHI 2.0 replaces it with a four-pillar, data-driven index graded against Mike's own baseline: 100 means "normal for Mike" (his 2023–2025 average).

This is a methodology change handled the way a statistical agency handles one: the old series is preserved intact as PHI-Classic, the new series is re-based to a documented baseline, and the two are shown side by side so the change is transparent. The headline number moves from PHI-Classic's 119.5 to PHI 2.0's 108 — that is a change of scale, not of health.

sections.title: Old PHI vs. New PHI
sections.body: Both indices tell the same story through late 2025 and 2026 — a dip into the winter, then a climb. They sit at different levels because they are measured on different scales: PHI-Classic on its own legacy baseline, PHI 2.0 re-based so that 100 equals Mike's 2023–2025 normal. The parallel trajectory is the point: the rebuild sharpened the resolution without inventing a different history.

sections.title: Why the headline moved from 119.5 to 108
sections.body: Nothing declined. PHI-Classic and PHI 2.0 are different rulers. PHI-Classic's 119.5 was a number on an open-ended legacy scale; PHI 2.0's 108 means "8% above Mike's normal," because the index is now anchored so that the 2023–2025 average is exactly 100. Re-basing to a fixed baseline is standard index practice (it is why the Consumer Price Index has a base year) — it makes every future number instantly legible: above 100 is better than normal, below is worse.

sections.title: The four pillars
sections.body:
Recovery (30%) — heart-rate variability and resting heart rate: is the body rested and firing.
Sleep (25%) — hours slept and night-to-night consistency.
Activity (25%) — energy burned, steps, and exercise minutes.
Fitness (20%) — VO2 max and cardio recovery, the long-run cardio-capacity signal.

Each pillar is scored against Mike's own 2023–2025 baseline and combined by the weights above. A drop in the headline with Activity down tells a different story than a drop with Recovery down — and the quarterly notes on the series page say which.

sections.title: What the rebuilt series shows
sections.body: With history now reaching back to 2023, PHI 2.0 surfaces a real inflection: a decline through the second half of 2025 that bottomed in the fourth quarter — a period when a relocation disrupted the training routine — followed by the strongest quarter on record in mid-2026. Where a single month was extreme enough to hit the index's floor, the quarterly note says so, so the headline never understates a story quietly.

outlook.title: Reading PHI Going Forward
outlook.body: PHI is published monthly, rolled up quarterly, with a one- or two-line note on each quarter explaining the move. 100 always means Mike's 2023–2025 normal, so the number is comparable across time. The full method — pillars, weights, normalization, and the base period — is open and documented. PHI-Classic remains available as the historical vintage.
